report:
**Conclusion:** Your skepticism is broadly justified. Whole-body vibration (WBV) should **not currently be considered a proven treatment to prevent osteoporotic fractures**.

The best direct evidence is a systematic review/meta-analysis of randomized trials in adults aged 50+ that evaluated falls, fractures, and bone outcomes. It found that WBV may reduce falls in some older populations, but fracture events were too few and evidence too limited/uncertain to establish a fracture-prevention benefit. A reduction in falls is not equivalent to demonstrated prevention of fragility fractures.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29289937/

Evidence in women with postmenopausal osteoporosis more commonly assesses *surrogate outcomes*—such as bone mineral density (BMD), muscle performance, balance, or gait—rather than actual fractures. Individual trials have reported BMD or functional improvements, but these do not demonstrate fewer fractures.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32868028/

The UK National Osteoporosis Guideline Group’s current non-drug guidance states that whole-body vibration has been shown to reduce fall rate but **does not increase BMD**. It does not present WBV as an established anti-fracture therapy.  
https://www.nogg.org.uk/full-guideline/section-5-non-pharmacological-management-osteoporosis

So, WBV might be a supplementary, supervised exercise option for balance or fall-risk reduction in selected people, but it should not replace therapies with demonstrated fracture reduction (appropriate osteoporosis medicines, resistance/weight-bearing and balance exercise, calcium/vitamin D when indicated, and fall-prevention measures). Discuss suitability and safety with the clinician managing the osteoporosis, especially after vertebral, hip, or other fragility fractures.
